query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a targeted, low-temperature thermomechanical treatment combined with a minor alloying addition designed to promote the nucleation of coherent nanoscale precipitates at the inter-lamellar interfaces will simultaneously reduce microcrack initiation and enhance dislocation pinning, thereby improving both the strength and tensile ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting abundant internal (colony and interphase) boundaries that concentrate stress and serve as microcrack initiation sites.
generation.intervention: Apply a low-temperature thermomechanical treatment combined with a strategically chosen minor alloying addition to induce coherent nanoscale precipitates along the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: The treatment must be executed at temperatures low enough to avoid precipitate coarsening or deleterious phase transformations, and the precipitate volume fraction and distribution must be carefully optimized for interface stabilization.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoscale secondary precipitates localized at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates are expected to pin dislocations and relieve local residual stresses, which reduces stress concentration at the interfaces and delays microcrack formation. This, in turn, promotes beneficial strain hardening and enhances the overall ductility, while also contributing to increased strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, the treated alloy should exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths alongside improved room-temperature ductility, evidenced by delayed microcrack initiation and enhanced dislocation storage and mobility.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloys with lamellar colonies that, while strong, experience brittle failure due to microcrack propagation along their numerous internal interfaces.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the processing temperature remains low enough to prevent precipitate coarsening, and if the introduced precipitates are uniformly distributed without causing embrittlement; deviations beyond these limits may negate the intended improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters and the specific choice of alloying element require further experimental determination, and there is inherent uncertainty in balancing the precipitate-induced strengthening with the need to maintain ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloy samples; one set will receive the targeted low-temperature thermomechanical treatment with the minor alloy addition, while the control set remains unmodified. Subject both sets to room-temperature tensile testing and microstructural characterization using electron microscopy to assess precipitate distribution and interface integrity.
measurements: Electron microscopy analysis of interfacial precipitate size, distribution, and coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility (or if ductility is reduced) compared to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

frame.goal: Achieve a simultaneous improvement in both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility, overcoming the trade‐off imposed by conventional processing.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing and many prior microstructural‐design strategies tend to improve strength at the expense of ductility or fail to eliminate brittle behavior (microcracking) originating at the numerous internal boundaries.

frame.understanding: The hypothesis addresses the need to modify the interphase boundary behavior to mitigate stress concentration and microcrack initiation while also promoting dislocation storage or accommodation, so that the overall alloy can yield under tensile load with enhanced strain hardening and delayed failure.
frame.proposed_hypothesis: Introducing an interfacial engineering intervention via a targeted, low-temperature thermomechanical treatment coupled with a minor alloying addition that promotes the nucleation of coherent, nanoscale secondary precipitates along the lamellar interfaces will simultaneously strengthen the internal boundaries and increase their fracture resistance. Mechanistically, the nanoscale precipitates will pin dislocations and provide a barrier to crack propagation while relieving residual stresses at the interfaces. It is predicted that compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline, treated samples will show higher yield and ultimate strengths along with increased tensile ductility by delaying the onset of microcracking. The boundary conditions include processing below the temperature where coarsening or deleterious phase transformations occur, and the volume fraction and distribution of precipitates must be optimized. Prior evidence from studies on grain boundary engineering in duplex alloys and high-entropy systems supports the potential of interface-stabilization strategies. An experiment that could falsify this hypothesis is to perform the specific interfacial treatment and then subject samples to room-temperature tensile tests; if such samples do not exhibit simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility (or if ductility degrades further) relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis would be refuted.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic HEAs (PMC4145285) demonstrated that a dual‐phase, lamellar microstructure combining soft FCC and hard B2 (or L12) phases can yield high strength with good ductility. Later studies then employed severe thermomechanical treatments (cryo‐rolling and annealing as in PMC5818523, and further refinement strategies in PMC6353877 and PMC6687781) to introduce hierarchical and ultrafine-grained structures aimed at further enhancing the strength–ductility balance. Although these approaches refined the microstructure and provided increased strength and controlled strain hardening, none directly addressed the role of the abundant internal (colony and interphase) boundaries in instigating microcrack formation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
decision.unsolved: The remaining challenge is to mitigate and stabilize the internal boundary regions of the lamellar colonies, which serve as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites. In spite of multiple processing routes to tune relative phase fractions and grain sizes, the intrinsic microstructural architecture has not been modified at the interface level to both impede crack propagation and promote beneficial dislocation mechanisms.
decision.lever: Implement a targeted, low-temperature thermomechanical treatment—possibly combined with a minor, strategically chosen alloying addition—to promote the nucleation of coherent, nanoscale secondary precipitates along the lamellar interfaces.
decision.why: Such an intervention builds directly on the trend of using thermomechanical processing for microstructural refinement but takes a more focused approach by engineering the internal boundaries. The proposed coherent nanoprecipitates would act to pin dislocations, relieve local residual stresses, and blunt stress concentration effects, thereby mitigating microcracking while enhancing both strength and ductility. Prior evidence from grain boundary engineering in duplex and refractory HEAs supports that coherent interfacial precipitates can improve crack resistance without sacrificing the beneficial lamellar colony structure.
